questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating an Integral Given Another Integral With Reversed Limits of Integration
questions.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{5}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{5}^{3}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=5.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factoring out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{5}(5-4f(x))\,\text{d}x & =5{\int }_{3}^{5}\text{d}x-4{\int }_{3}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\cdot x{|}_{3}^{5}-4(5) \\  & =5(5-3)-20 \\  & =10-20 \\  & =-10.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Definite Integral Given Integrals Over Adjacent Intervals
questions.problem: Given that ${\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-2$ and ${\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x=3,$ then what is ${\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)+2)\,\text{d}x?$
questions.worked_solution:
From the adjacent intervals rule, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in the known information into the above gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2+3 & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ 1 & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute the desired integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)+2)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x+2{\int }_{0}^{3}\text{d}x \\  & =1+2\cdot x\,{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =1+2(3-0) \\  & =1+6 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating an Integral Given Another Integral With Reversed Limits of Integration
questions.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{6}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{6}^{1}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=7\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factor out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{6}(2f(x)-1)\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{1}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x\,-\,{\int }_{1}^{6}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2(7)\,-\,x\,{|}_{1}^{6} \\  & =14\,-\,(6-1) \\  & =14\,-\,5 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Definite Integral Using Multiple Properties of Definite Integrals
questions.worked_solution:
Let's simplify one of the given integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{7}^{2}(-5)\,f(x)\,\text{d}x & =15 \\ (-5){\int }_{7}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =15 \\ 5{\int }_{2}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =15 \\ {\int }_{2}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Then, from the adjacent intervals rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =1+3 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Definite Integral Using Multiple Properties of Definite Integrals
questions.worked_solution:
Let's simplify one of the given integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{8}\frac{1}{2}\,g(x)\,\text{d}x & =-4 \\ \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{8}g(x)\,\text{d}x & =-4 \\ {\int }_{0}^{8}g(x)\,\text{d}x & =-8\end{aligned}
$$

Using the adjacent intervals rule and substituting known values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{8}(3f(x)+g(x))\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(3f(x)+g(x))\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{8}(3f(x)+g(x))\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

By the sum rule for definite integrals,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{8}(3f(x)+g(x))\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{0}^{8}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{8}g(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3(9)+(-8) \\  & =19.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}(3f(x)+g(x))\,\text{d}x & =19-{\int }_{3}^{8}(3f(x)+g(x))\,\text{d}x \\  & =19-10 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$
